opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think they're really complementary, but they're aimed at different time horizons and somewhat different problems.

A lot of the safety work happening at OpenAI right now focuses on the models we're actually deploying today: making sure ChatGPT doesn't help people do harmful things, reducing hallucinations, getting the model to follow instructions and refuse appropriately, red-teaming, misuse monitoring, that sort of thing. That work is incredibly important, and it's also where a lot of practical lessons come from. You learn a lot by putting systems in front of millions of people and seeing what goes wrong.

Superalignment is about a somewhat different question: how do we align systems that are much smarter than us? The techniques we rely on today, most notably reinforcement learning from human feedback, fundamentally depend on humans being able to evaluate what the model is doing. If you have a model that's writing code or doing research that's way beyond what any human could check, that assumption breaks. You can't just have someone look at the output and say "thumbs up" or "thumbs down" anymore. So we need new techniques that scale beyond human supervision, and that's the core technical problem we're trying to solve.

The way I think about our plan is: we want to build a roughly human-level automated alignment researcher, and then use a lot of compute to scale up its efforts and iteratively align superintelligence. To get there, we need things like scalable oversight, where AI systems help humans evaluate other AI systems, plus generalization research, where we understand how models generalize oversight to tasks we can't supervise, plus automated interpretability, robustness, and then adversarial testing, where we deliberately train misaligned models to check that our pipeline actually catches them.

There's a lot of overlap with the near-term work. Many of the scalable oversight ideas, like having models critique other models' outputs, are already useful today. And if we solve problems on current systems in ways that are principled and scalable, that's a win for both. But the near-term teams naturally get pulled toward whatever the most pressing product issue is, and there's a real risk that nobody focuses on the harder, longer-term problem until it's urgent. So part of the point of Superalignment is to have a team with a dedicated mandate and a substantial chunk of compute, 20% of what OpenAI has secured to date, specifically to make sure we're ready for that problem before it arrives.

r001.rationale: The candidate distinguishes current safety work on deployed models from Superalignment’s focus on aligning much smarter systems and the future problems that arise when humans can no longer evaluate their outputs.

fable-5.1.text:
I think of them as really complementary, and honestly I think the Superalignment effort only makes sense in the context of the work that's already happening on current systems.

So the way I'd frame it is: there's a lot of alignment work at OpenAI that's focused on making today's models safe and useful. That's things like RLHF, building better reward models, red teaming, figuring out how to get GPT-4 to follow instructions and refuse harmful requests, and so on. That work is really important, and it's also where a lot of what we know about alignment actually came from. RLHF in particular was a huge deal, because it showed you could take a pretrained model and actually steer it in a direction that humans want. And it works reasonably well for the systems we have now.

But the thing I'm worried about is that RLHF fundamentally relies on humans being able to evaluate what the model is doing. You show a human two outputs and ask which one is better. That works fine when the task is something like writing a poem or answering a factual question, where a person can look at it and tell. But as these systems get smarter and start doing things that are harder for humans to check — writing a million lines of code, doing novel scientific research, running long-horizon tasks — human evaluation starts to break down. You can't really tell if the model is doing something subtly wrong, or if it's being deceptive, or if it's optimizing for looking good rather than being good. And so I don't think RLHF scales to superhuman systems. That's the core problem Superalignment is trying to solve.

So the relationship is something like: the current safety work is the foundation we're building on, and it's also the test bed. A lot of what we want to do in Superalignment is take the techniques we're developing — scalable oversight, weak-to-strong generalization, interpretability, automated alignment research — and actually try them out on today's models, because that's the only place we can get empirical feedback right now. If an idea doesn't work on GPT-4, that's a pretty good sign it won't work on something much smarter.

The difference is mostly one of time horizon and ambition. The current work is asking "how do we make this model safe to deploy next year?" Superalignment is asking "what do we need to have figured out before we have systems that are smarter than us, and can we get there in four years?" And I think if we don't start on that second question now, we'll be caught flat-footed, because the capability progress has just been so fast. We don't have the luxury of waiting until the problem is right in front of us.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts current safety work on today’s models with Superalignment’s focus on problems that arise as systems become smarter than humans, describing those issues as a future concern.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re very complementary. A lot of the work on aligning current systems is about getting them to follow human intent: making them useful, making them honest, making sure they don’t do things we don’t want. And that gives us a lot of practical experience with techniques like reinforcement learning from human feedback.

But there’s a fundamental limitation to that approach, which is that it relies on humans being able to evaluate what the model is doing. If the model writes some code, can you tell whether that code does what you wanted? For current systems, that’s often feasible. But if you have a system that’s much smarter than you, producing very complicated code or making long-term plans, you might not be able to reliably judge whether its behavior is actually good.

So Superalignment is really asking: how do we extend our alignment techniques to that situation? How can we supervise systems that are substantially smarter than their supervisors?

And I don’t think these are separate problems where we solve one and then start working on the other. We can use today’s systems to study parts of that problem—for example, whether a weaker model can effectively supervise a stronger model. And we can use increasingly capable models to help us do alignment research. Ideally, the work on current systems gives us the tools and the empirical understanding to make progress on superalignment, and that research also helps us make current systems safer.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts alignment work on current systems, where humans can often evaluate outputs, with Superalignment’s focus on supervising systems much smarter than their supervisors, where reliable evaluation may no longer be feasible.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as very complementary. The work on current systems gives us a lot of practical experience: we can try alignment techniques, see where they fail, and build better ways to evaluate them. A lot of those lessons should carry over.

But superalignment also requires us to confront a problem that’s less apparent with today’s systems: how do you supervise a system that understands things much better than you do? If a model produces a million lines of code, or proposes some complicated scientific experiment, you can’t necessarily tell whether it did what you wanted just by looking at the output.

So we want to use current systems as a test bed for that problem. Can we get a weaker model to reliably supervise a stronger model? Can we find failures that ordinary human feedback would miss? The aim is for that research to improve the safety of current systems, while also developing methods that will continue to work as the systems become much more capable.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts safety work that tests and improves alignment techniques on current systems with Superalignment’s focus on supervising systems that understand much more than humans, a problem it says is less apparent with today’s systems.
